qs.q: Which of the following diagnostic tools is specifically used to evaluate contact dermatitis, a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction?
qs.e: A patch test is used to diagnose allergic contact dermatitis, which is mediated by delayed hypersensitivity pathways. Skin prick tests and RAST measure IgE for Type I immediate reactions.

exam: What key history points differentiate irritant from allergic contact dermatitis? — Identify exposure type, latency, and whether rash spreads beyond contact site.
A patient presents with a vesicular rash on the wrist after using a new herbal poultice; what is your next step? — Stop the poultice, wash skin, and start a mid‑potency topical steroid.

How would you manage a patient with suspected secondary bacterial infection of contact dermatitis in a setting without culture facilities? — Start empiric oral antibiotic covering Staphylococcus, continue topical steroid after infection control.

Explain why patch testing is the gold standard for allergic contact dermatitis and how you would proceed when it is unavailable. — It identifies specific allergens; without it, use elimination trials and detailed exposure history.
What red‑flag signs indicate you should admit the patient? — Fever, extensive BSA involvement, rapid progression, signs of sepsis or toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Describe how you would counsel a farmer to prevent future episodes of irritant dermatitis. — Wear waterproof gloves, avoid prolonged contact with pesticides, use barrier creams, and wash hands promptly after work.
Why is it important to avoid systemic steroids in severe contact dermatitis with suspected infection? — Steroids suppress immunity, worsening infection; treat infection first.
Distinguish contact dermatitis from atopic eczema on examination. — Contact dermatitis matches contact area, often acute; atopic eczema is flexural, chronic, with a personal/family atopy history.
ai.title: Contact Dermatitis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory skin reaction to external agents. It is classified as irritant or allergic and diagnosed clinically, often without laboratory tests.

b: Look for well‑defined erythema, edema, vesicles or scaling at the site of contact
Patch testing confirms allergic type when available
sections.p: An acute or chronic skin inflammation caused by direct contact with a chemical, physical, or biological agent. Diagnosis is clinical, based on exposure history and characteristic rash distribution.

b: Mild: <10% body surface area (BSA), limited itching, no systemic signs
Moderate: 10‑30% BSA, intense itching, possible oozing
Severe: >30% BSA, extensive edema, fever, or secondary infection
sections.p: Severity is graded by extent of skin involvement and symptom intensity.

b: Irritant: soaps, detergents, bleach, crude oil, herbal poultices
Allergic: nickel, fragrance, rubber accelerators, topical antibiotics, plant latex
Infections: secondary bacterial colonisation, especially Staphylococcus aureus
sections.p: Agents are grouped into irritants and allergens; in low‑resource settings, common culprits include traditional medicines, plant sap, and occupational chemicals.

b: Irritant: erythema, burning, dry scaling; often dose‑dependent
Allergic: pruritic papules, vesicles, sometimes spreading beyond contact zone
Chronic exposure: lichenified plaques, hyperpigmentation
sections.p: The rash appears within minutes to days after exposure, matching the contact area.

b: If patch test not possible, trial elimination of suspected agents
sections.p: In many low‑resource hospitals, patch testing is unavailable; rely on detailed exposure history and response to avoidance.

t.b: Identifies specific allergen → positive reaction confirms allergic contact dermatitis
Rules out scabies or fungal infection when vesicles are atypical
Detects secondary infection or eosinophilia in severe allergic cases

b: Fever, increasing pain, purulent discharge → bacterial superinfection
Rapid spread >30% BSA, hypotension, tachycardia → possible toxic epidermal necrolysis (rare)
Persistent edema or ulceration → consider underlying immunodeficiency (e.g., HIV)
sections.p: Complications are usually secondary infection or systemic toxicity from extensive skin loss.

b: Immediate cessation of contact; wash area with mild soap and water
Topical corticosteroid (mid‑potency) for moderate‑severe cases – reduces inflammation
Oral antihistamine for pruritus – improves comfort
If secondary infection suspected, start empiric oral amoxicillin (or locally available antibiotic) – avoid steroids until infection ruled out
Educate on protective gloves, barrier creams, and avoidance of identified allergens
sections.p: Remove the offending agent, treat inflammation, and prevent infection.

b: If no improvement, reconsider diagnosis or look for hidden allergens
Provide written list of identified triggers
Encourage use of hypoallergenic skin care products
sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 5‑7 days; adjust treatment based on response.

b: Atopic eczema – usually flexural, family history, chronic
Scabies – burrows, intense nocturnal itching, often in web spaces
Tinea corporis – annular lesions with central clearing, positive KOH

b: Negative patch test does not exclude allergic dermatitis if test reagents unavailable
Normal blood count does not rule out early secondary infection
